mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Condition jointly on Team A's shots FOR (long-run vs. recent-5) and Team A's shots_on_target FOR (long-run vs. recent-5) to compute a within-team shot-quality ratio, then cross it against Team B's shots_on_target AGAINST (long-run vs. recent-5). Both the ratio dimension and the opponent-allowed dimension must be active simultaneously — not one at a time.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When a team's recent shots-on-target share falls well below its long-run share while its raw shot volume holds steady, its effective on-target output against a given opponent's allowed rate is suppressed relative to what raw shot volume alone would predict.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A's shot volume is substantially higher than Team B's shots-allowed rate, yet Team A's shots-on-target rate has dropped sharply in recent matches relative to its long-run average. The joint relationship between Team A's shot volume and its shots-on-target conversion rate (shots-on-target as a share of shots) — measured across both long-run and recent windows simultaneously — conditions how many on-target attempts Team A actually generates against Team B's defensive profile.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires a joint ratio of two distinct observables (shots and shots_on_target) for the same team, compared across two time windows simultaneously, then crossed against the opponent's allowed rate — three dimensions active at once. No single-observable mirror or single-band split covers this.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on Team B's shots FOR and shots_on_target FOR against Team A's shots AGAINST and shots_on_target AGAINST. The mechanism is asymmetric: Team B's offensive ratio is compared against Team A's defensive ratio, not the same observable mirrored.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When the attacking team's shots-on-target share exceeds the defending team's shots-on-target-allowed share, the on-target volume advantage rises faster than the raw shot volume gap alone would suggest.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team B generates substantially more shots than Team A allows on average, yet Team B's shots-on-target FOR (long-run) is also higher than Team A's shots-on-target AGAINST (long-run). The asymmetric cross between Team B's offensive shot profile (shots FOR and shots_on_target FOR) and Team A's defensive shot-quality profile (shots AGAINST and shots_on_target AGAINST) — where the two observables are different for each side — determines whether Team B's volume advantage translates into a proportional on-target advantage.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This is an asymmetric cross of two distinct observables across two sides simultaneously — not a single-observable mirror. It requires computing ratios for both teams on different observables and comparing them jointly.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on Team A's fouls FOR (long-run vs. recent-5 divergence) and Team B's fouls AGAINST (long-run vs. recent-5 divergence), then relate this joint foul-pressure signal to the combined corner-kick production of both teams (Team A corners FOR + Team B corners FOR). The two observables — fouls and corners — must be linked jointly, not independently.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When the attacking team's recent foul rate falls while the defending team's recent foul-concession rate rises, the corner-kick volume is elevated relative to what each team's corner average alone would predict, because defensive pressure and set-piece frequency co-move with foul patterns.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team A commits fouls at a high long-run rate but its recent-5 foul rate has dropped sharply, while Team B's fouls-against rate has risen recently. The joint relationship between Team A's foul production (FOR) and Team B's foul-concession rate (AGAINST) — each measured across both long-run and recent windows — conditions the expected corner-kick volume, since fouls near the box and defensive pressure are linked to corner generation. Specifically, when one team's foul rate diverges across windows while the opponent's foul-allowed rate diverges in the opposite direction, the corner-kick total is affected in a non-additive way.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This involves a genuine joint relationship between two distinct observables (fouls and corner_kicks) across both teams, with a within-team recent-vs-long-run divergence dimension active simultaneously. It cannot be reduced to a single observable with one conditioning band.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Jointly condition on Team A's yellow_cards FOR (long-run) and Team B's yellow_cards FOR (long-run), together with both teams' fouls FOR rates, to assess whether the combined foul-and-card pressure environment predicts elevated cards_2h beyond what either team's cards_2h rate alone would indicate. The mechanism requires all three observables active simultaneously across both teams.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When both teams independently show above-context yellow-card and foul rates, the second-half cards total rises above what either team's cards_2h rate alone predicts — a super-additive joint effect.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: The second-half cards rate (cards_2h) for both teams is substantially above the competition context mean, and both teams show elevated yellow-card rates. The joint relationship between a team's yellow-card accumulation rate (full-match) and its second-half cards rate — conditioned on the opponent's yellow-card production rate — captures whether card escalation in the second half is driven by a structural tendency of both teams to foul heavily and accumulate cards together, rather than by either team's card rate in isolation.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This is a joint relationship among three distinct observables (cards_2h, yellow_cards, fouls) across both teams simultaneously, not a single-observable mirror or single-band split. The super-additivity hypothesis requires measuring the joint distribution, not each observable independently.

mechanisms.conditioning_logic: Condition jointly on Team A's corner_kicks FOR in FIRST_HALF and SECOND_HALF separately, crossed against Team B's corner_kicks AGAINST in FIRST_HALF and SECOND_HALF separately. This requires within-match half-level resolution for both the attacking and defending side simultaneously — two half-splits active at once across two teams.
mechanisms.expected_relationship_to_test: When the attacking team's corner production is more concentrated in the second half and the defending team's corner-concession rate is also higher in the second half, the second-half corner total rises disproportionately relative to the first half, beyond what either team's full-match corner average would predict.
mechanisms.mechanism_statement: Team B concedes corners at a substantially higher rate than Team A generates them, and Team B's corners-against rate has risen further in recent matches. Simultaneously, Team A's corner generation is split asymmetrically across halves (first-half vs. second-half). The joint relationship between Team A's half-level corner production profile (first-half FOR vs. second-half FOR) and Team B's half-level corner-concession profile (first-half AGAINST vs. second-half AGAINST) — measured within the same match — determines whether the corner advantage is concentrated in one half or distributed across both.
mechanisms.why_not_baseline_equivalent: This requires within-match half-level splits for both teams simultaneously on the same observable — a two-dimensional half-split across two sides. No single-observable single-band split covers this; the engine's supported two-way splits do not include two half-splits across two teams at once.
